verdict.tagline: Deep colony management wrapped in cute visuals with brutal learning curves.
for_you_if: you enjoy intricate system building and thermodynamics
you like steep learning curves and complex problem solving
not_for_you_if: you rely heavily on in-game tutorials
you are frustrated by pathing bugs and crashing issues
you prefer straightforward survival games without external guides

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as complex and challenging with a steep learning curve, requiring external tutorials or guides to understand mechanics during the early hours.

citations.review_text: its amazing! at first i thought it would be boring, but after playing with the guidance of video tutorial, i find it close to real life!
A lack of in game tutorial makes this for a challenging / boring play
It's a really hard game, with lot of things to find out about it and the learning curve is not smooth. I had to search some tutorials to being with. But it's so fun. Tons of things to do.
It's a fun game to play, It is hard to understand all the mechanics of the game but after a few YT Guides you'll be good to go.

This is a great game and you can very quicky spend alot of time playing it. One issue I have come across is there is little to no tutorial and you are just thrown into the game for the first few times and need to search a lot up. Other than that great game love the mechanics.

[h3]Not for everyone[/h3]

ONI is one of those games where the difficulty curve is a steep mountain. To be successful, you are expected to have prior knowledge about positioning, logistics, consumption and production. A mistake in the early game can easily ruin hours of work, something you notice only once people start dieing in droves.

I found the tutorlals not up to the task. They stop just before important parts like oxygen/food/energy production. There are also no milestones beyond long term goals, which means the player isn't even given a nudge about what should be done next.

This game is super fun, its all about problem solving and management. Especially gas management. It really gets you thinking. I also appreciate the hands-off approach with not too many overbearing tutorials at the beginning. You get to experiment in order to learn. And of course, have google/reddit by your side to help out when you're stuck!

It's complicated. I like the cartoony style, but man this games stressful. 

Was expecting a simple colony sim game, but was met with hardcore auditing instead.

The game is just not well explained to my simple brain I guess. It's like Don't Starve Together. You need to have watched/read several guides on what to do, covering the multi stage processes you need to accomplish or you die. You need to know a plan before you play, since it won't tell you what stuff is or does or that you need it. But unlike DST, this one's all about building optimal tile sets and the idea of the game is to what? renewably produce oxygen?  
IDK, ain't for me

cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Expanding bases requires mastering interconnected ventilation and plumbing while dealing with character pathing loops.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe pathing and AI issues where characters get stuck in loops, trap themselves in corners, or starve because they cannot navigate properly.

citations.review_text: Haven't played it in quite some time, wanted to try again, but realized that the only things I remember about it is how tiresome and frustrating it was. The last time I quit was because of a pathing issue where characters got stuck in a loop of climbing a ladder, moving a single block, falling down, climbing up again.

This is a very challenging game! Maintaining a small area is relatively easy, but the game kinda forces you to expand. The more you expand, the more you have to deal with...

Make the area too big, and it becomes difficult to sustain oxygen levels.. same for if you start having lots of living things that use the oxygen and let out CO2..

Areas can get super hot, super cold... wet areas carry lots of germs.. plumbing.. air circulation and vacuum seals.. creature farms..

One of my biggest issues with this game is, however, when you start automating stuff as you scale. Your works can randomly lock themselves in some corner of the map after build something and that's it.. they just get stuck there starving, drowning, cold.. by the time you notice, they are either almost dead and so far away that sometimes by the time someone comes to save them, they died...

Basically, the AI is stupid and locks itself in corners occasionally and dies for no reason... and this can very much ruin a whole save sometimes..

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game has a steep learning curve and requires managing complex interconnected systems such as plumbing, gas flow, ventilation, temperature, and automation.

citations.review_text:
Started a colony. I forgot what my characters' traits even were but research was slow. They were peeing everywhere, and there was that looming black smoke somewhere on the right. My water supply was slowly but very surely turning green. Eventually learned about priorities, scheduling, plumbing and ventilation. My colony was still miraculously surviving, but I felt overwhelmed trying to save them.

I created a new colony. Started looking up guides. Read through wiki. Was honestly getting the hang of it and I thought I could finally pat myself on the back. Then I accidentally dug up a volcano. There were also materials by said volcano, and the duplicates were trying to get to those materials for storage (I didn't even tell them to). For some weird reason, didn't even check up on temperature. Until it was too late. My hospitals suddenly started to get full, and nearby equipment was melting. Eventually realized I still can't have that pat.

But I decided to stick with this colony. The cycle before I dug the volcano was still in the save option so I reloaded that save file. Had to say goodbye to Bubbles though- I had hastily picked her after volcano was dug up. I thought her 'medicine' trait could help. Anyway. I decided to not dig the volcano just yet. Had to cancel all the dig tasks near it. But now I have another problem. My power was shutting down. Coal was running out fast. I picked another Bubbles, but she's good at husbandry this time. Hopefully the Hatches can save me. Otherwise..... I think I might really have to dig that volcano.

Overall- the game can be a bit "stressful". But somehow, seeing them duplicates' eyes lighting up and clapping whenever a research is done, or just being happy receiving a new hat (blissfully unaware some part or another in the colony is failing real hard and real fast), I feel compelled to not give up.
complicated but a good type of complicated

If you’re on the fence about this game, do yourself a huge favor and get it. I’m only a few sessions in — three, to be exact — and I already have 27 hours. That alone should tell you how quickly this game grabs you. I’ve played a lot of colony survival games over the years, but this one… this one became my favorite the moment I booted it up.

I first discovered Oxygen Not Included as a kid watching Markiplier stumble through his early colonies on YouTube. Even back then, something about it stuck with me — the charm, the chaos, the way every tiny system mattered. Coming back to it now as an adult, it feels even better than I remembered.

What makes this game special is how simple it feels at first, and how beautifully complex it becomes as you learn. Not the kind of complexity that overwhelms you — the kind that invites you deeper. You start with a few dupes digging out a tiny pocket of rock, and before you know it you’re managing heat, plumbing, oxygen flow, food production, stress levels, automation, and somehow it all feels natural. Every problem is a puzzle, and every solution feels like a small victory.

There’s this moment every player hits — where your base is humming, your dupes are thriving, and you realize you’ve built something that feels alive. That’s when the game really shines. It’s not just survival; it’s creativity, engineering, and storytelling all wrapped together.

The art style is charming, the humor is subtle, the systems are deep, and the sense of progression is incredibly satisfying. Even when things go wrong (and trust me, they will), it never feels unfair. It feels like learning. It feels like discovery.

I absolutely recommend this game 100%. If you enjoy colony sims, survival management, or just watching tiny cartoon people panic because you forgot to build a toilet, this game is worth every minute.

I can’t wait to dive into the DLCs next — if they’re anything like the base game, I’m in for dozens more hours of pure, delightful…

I eat cereal for lunch. Or atleast I do now cuz I don't get time to make food cuz of this game. Oni is complex. There is no denying that. Yes, it has an insane learning curve, which scared me at first too, and yes, even if you learn everything properly, it can feel boring at times; but oni is, in my opinion atleast, one of the most relatable games out there. It is a sandbox but unlike other sandboxes I've tried where I feel bored after a few play throughs, oni genuinely feels exciting to me. Tho this is my first sandbox colony management game (I haven't played games like factories, dwarf fortress, rimworld etc) so I might be exaggerating on stuff that is basically common to all such games.
What I liked:
Brain upgrade: You will spend so much time in this game literally staring at the screen and doing flipping math of all things that it's actually insane. You will probably increase your iq by a few points doing that. Jokes aside tho, oni really makes you think. There is no plug and play solution that works everywhere. You'd be lucky if a few "modifications" to a popular build or method is all you need to make it work.
Im an idiot: Player accountability in the game is basically 100%. Oni doesn't speak enemies randomly or try to drown your dupes. You do. The black unknown in oni unfolds as you explore. You have plenty of time to correct any mistakes. Lost water? Maybe you didn't notice that the whole greenhouse bristle blossoms is taking over 400kg water per cycle. Base getting hot? How about you stop running 10 industrial machines right next to the crops? Lost oxygen? Why didn't you pay attention to your algae supplies? Every failure of the colony is on you and you alone. (Tho I admit dupes will try their very best to screw themselves over all the time)
Flipping math: nothing in this game is easy without it. Want food? Calculate the food given by your plants per cycle and divide by 1000. That's how many crops you need....FOR 1 DUPE!!! Oh, want to use electrolyzers …

In my opinion, this the game that have many content and important if you choose survival mode you need to think and plan to make your Duplicant survive some function are hard to understand at first but trust me if you learning and doing you enjoy this game.

It's a pretty interesting game. Most of the game has you managing gas, liquid, and temperature for your colony. There are restrictions in how you handle these things that do tend to mirror the real world which makes it an interesting puzzle to solve. It is a brutally hard game, but rewarding when you figure something out. There doesn't seem to be too much of an overarching goal, although you can "beat" the game. I'd say this game is in the same vein as Dwarf Fortress, you manage your citizens and make sure they don't run out of food and oxygen. That may sound simple, but the game is rife with unforeseen consequences.

cohorts.label: 100h+
cohorts.summary: Long-term players master deep thermodynamics and gas management, though some experience frustrating crashes during autosaves.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features deep plumbing, gas, heat management, and thermodynamics mechanics that require careful system building.

citations.review_text:
Oxygen Not Included is one of those games that looks fairly simple at first, then suddenly you realise you’ve spent three hours redesigning a plumbing system because someone peed in the clean water supply.

The amount of depth here is ridiculous. You start out worrying about food and oxygen, but before long you’re dealing with heat management, gas pressure, power grids, automation, germs, liquid loops and increasingly elaborate systems designed to stop your colony from killing itself.

What I really like is that failure rarely feels completely random. Normally something goes wrong because of a decision you made 20 cycles ago that has finally come back to haunt you.

There’s definitely a learning curve, and the game isn't particularly forgiving when you're starting out. You’ll probably restart multiple colonies as you realise everything you did in the previous one was horribly inefficient. But learning how everything interacts is a huge part of the fun.

It’s basically an engineering problem disguised as a cute colony simulator, and if you enjoy building systems, optimising things and solving problems, it’s dangerously addictive.

I came for the cute cartoons. I stayed because I now have a PhD in applied thermodynamics.

Expectation: A relaxing colony sim where you make sure cute little clones have enough air and don't pee in the water supply.

Reality (200+ hours in): I am actively exploiting the specific gravity of liquids, relying on the fact that crude oil naturally sinks below water, just to build the perfect vacuum airlock.

I currently care more about the exact reproduction metrics and happiness levels of my Pacu fish than I do about my own real-world social life. If my fish aren't happy, the resource loop breaks, and we can't have that.

Also, bless the developers for making basic gas pipes cost raw ores instead of refined metals. I need every single ounce of refined metal for my massively over-engineered, fully automated kitchen and an infinite storage system that fundamentally violates the laws of physics.

Pros:
- Deep, satisfying plumbing and gas management mechanics.
- You will learn more about heat exchange than you did in high school.
- The Pacu fish are cute (even when you are meticulously calculating their optimal breeding conditions).

Cons:
- I close my eyes and just see overlays of ventilation pipes.

10/10. Would accidentally boil my entire colony alive while trying to perfectly automate a grill again.

I like life support game. ONI is a game of building systems, and it does that well.

The bathroom module I designed myself self-recycles the polluted water it produces and exhausts the excess into my oxygen module, the oxygen module cycles its output through my main water tank to cool down the output.
Everything you build in this game works better with other systems you build.

If you want a building game where you build and use your own stuff and exploit mechanics such as temperature, pressure, heat capacities, heat transfer rate, and solid -> liquid -> gas transitions look no further.

Been playing intermittently since early-access.

The potential is there, and this game even taught me a bit about thermodynamics.

But after nearly 1000 hours, I'm done with this game.

Every time I try a new colony, always something ends up ruining up.

And instead of adding quality-of-life improvements to make the early stages of the game playable, instead we get late-game stuff that you will never get to use anyway. Never in my 900 hours of gameplay did I reach the surface, let alone use rocket stuff. Only a few colonies actually managed to dig for oil and produce plastic.

The frustration comes from so many questionable decisions that you end up drowning the game in mods to fix them all, only for the game to not be able to handle it or having conflicting mods, not to mention updates breaking them as well.

Why is storing food a supply errand instead of a store errand??

How do you cool your colony down without constant blackouts due to insane power demands??

Why are there some pages of the in-game encyclopedia missing?? You click a link and it leads you to an in-game 404. Is this game even finished??

Why is the "best" way to seal gases to put a 1g puddle of water, instead of having actual airlocks??

Speaking of puddles, why do your people get hipothermia from stepping on their own pee as they clean it??

Why do sweepies not have a liquid output, thus causing stored liquids to be stored there forever??

Why do I have this "Long commutes" warning when you need to walk to get things done and delivered??

Maybe it's because my builder builds something, then waits around because someone from the other end of the colony is carrying the resouces needed to build the next thing, instead of having the builder "compete" for that task and grab a bunch of the several TONS of sandstone that I've stored nearby??

claims.claim: Reviewers state that progressing through the game effectively requires relying on external resources like online tutorials, wikis, or creative mode.

citations.review_text:
I don't like how this game is secretly a rogue-like with 30 hour run averages. I don't like having to learn a new system(example radiation) so far into a playthrough. The penalty for failing to fully understand and exploit these many systems results in a failed playthrough. It is almost a necessity to play around in creative mode around all the games bigger systems or watch tutorials before a successful normal playthrough can be attempted. Trial and error simply takes to long to be a valid way to play a game this long. However going to these extremes of using external resources really took away my ability to properly explore and lead with curiosity in the main game. I have the same fundamental issues with The Don't Starve Series.
On a positive note, the many in depth colony management systems really elevate this game to something special.
I like the game, there's a learning curve but honestly there's tons of online tutorials

Nearly 300 hours in and I've JUST built rockets. Played most of those hours on base game with no mods or DLC; only recently got all DLC (except Aquatic which wasn't out yet - excited for when I can grab it!) and started modding and this game just got a WHOLE LOT bigger.

Very active workshop and lots of community builds to explore (my personal favorite is "Easy Submerged Electrolyzer / SPOM Guide" by Magialisk). I highly recommend getting the DLCs if you have the money, but even base game has.. well.. hundreds of hours of content.

If you're a fan of RimWorld or other colony sims, you'll love Oxygen Not Included. This game is inherently a bit unforgiving but all difficulty settings are configurable. It's very fun to explore and figure out on your own but don't be afraid to look at the wiki or any community guides - they probably figured out something you haven't that'll be life changing.
